deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. It is a page of German lecture or study notes on ancient history, a continuation of the previous page on Cleopatra and Ptolemaic Egypt. It opens a new section: '3. Geschichte des macedonischen Reichs und der griechischen Staaten, 323–146' (History of the Macedonian empire and the Greek states, 323–146 BC).

The content, in order:
- After Alexander's death (323) the Greeks try to throw off Macedonian rule. Hyperides and Demosthenes are the 'souls' of a strong alliance, led by Athen.
- Athens' commander is Leosthenes. The writer first wrote Leonatus, struck it out and wrote Leosthenes in the margin.
- Antipater can field only 13,000 men against 30,000. He asks Leonnatus, 'governor of Mysia', for help, and Leonnatus comes.
- At first the Greeks win, and Antipater has to shut himself up in the fortress town of Lamia. The Greeks win a victory near Thermopylae and Leonnatus falls.
- Craterus then comes from Asia with part of the royal army. Leosthenes 'blieb' (fell) during the siege of Lamia.
- Demosthenes and Hyperides go into exile. Athens receives a Macedonian garrison and Phocion is at the head of affairs.
- After Perdiccas' death in 321, Antipater is appointed regent. A marginal note keyed by '+' to the date 320 reads: 'Er hinterließ einen Sohn Cassander' (he left a son, Cassander).
- He is succeeded by Polyperchon. After a four-year struggle, Cassander takes possession of Macedonia; the sentence continues on the next page.

The hand and genre (a student's notes on Heeren-style ancient-history lectures) suggest this sheet is bound into the Gauss bundle but is not a Gauss mathematical manuscript. It may not be in Gauss's hand at all; that is uncertain.
errors: Historical: Leonnatus was satrap of Hellespontine Phrygia; calling him governor of 'Mysia' is a loose approximation.
Historical: Leonnatus fell in a cavalry battle in Thessaly in 322 BC while marching to relieve Lamia, not literally at Thermopylae.
Historical: Leosthenes was killed early in the siege of Lamia, before Leonnatus' defeat. The notes reverse this order.
Historical: the notes omit the decisive Macedonian victory at Crannon (322 BC), which ended the Lamian War.
Historical: Hyperides was executed in 322 BC and Demosthenes committed suicide on Calauria the same year. 'Exile' understates this: they fled and then died.
Historical: the Macedonian garrison in Munychia was commanded by Menyllus. Phocion headed the oligarchic Athenian government, not the garrison.
Chronology: Antipater died in 319 BC; the marginal '320' follows an older chronology. Perdiccas' death is dated 321 or 320 depending on the chronology used.

results.what: Narrative notes on the Lamian War and the early Diadochi period (323–319 BC); no mathematical content
results.usually_credited_to: standard ancient-history curriculum, e.g. A. H. L. Heeren's Handbuch der Geschichte der Staaten des Alterthums

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds only routine historical lecture notes on Macedonia after Alexander, with no mathematical content. It is probably not even a Gauss mathematical manuscript.
transcription_corrections: Line 'das an [-Leonatus-]': in the image 'Leonatus' is struck through in the text line, and 'Leosthenes' is written in the left margin as its replacement.
'Termopylae' is spelled thus in the manuscript (for Thermopylae). 'Cratherus' and 'Leonathus' are the writer's spellings.
The marginal note 'Er hinterließ einen Sohn Cassander.' sits in the left margin, keyed by '+' to the '+320+' insertion before 'Ihm folgte Polysperchon'.
'Sie erfochten[?] den Sieg' is a plausible reading: 'erfochten den Sieg'.
'an deren Spit-ze[?]' is confirmed in the image as 'an deren Spit-ze Phocion stand'.
The end of the line after 'Polysperchon' ('kein[?] Er und[?]') is uncertain in the image. It probably introduces the Cassander–Polyperchon conflict; 'kein' is likely a misreading.
